skill.name: A setting built from the senses
skill.why: Readers can't see your world. Senses let them step inside it.
skill.how: Pick a place. Add what you'd hear, smell, touch and taste, not just see.

steps.say: I'm painting the school canteen, but I need words first. Here's my first try.

show.text: The canteen was big and had lots of tables.

steps.ask: Which sense does my line use?

options.reason: Is there any noise in it? Read it again.
Nothing smells in it. There is just big and tables.

steps.win: Right. Only sight. You can see the canteen, but you're not in it yet.

steps.say: So I added more. Read each line. Listen, sniff and feel.

show.text: The canteen hummed with kids slurping noodles.
The air stank of burnt toast.
show.nudge: You'd sniff that, not hear it. Which line makes a noise?

show.text: The benches were sticky with sauce.
show.nudge: You'd feel that on your skin. Which line makes a noise?

steps.ask: Tap the line you could hear.
steps.win: Yes! Humming and slurping are sounds. The other labels show smell and touch.

steps.say: Smell is the sense writers forget most. Here is the pool on a hot day.

show.nudge: You'd hear that one. Which line could you sniff?
You'd feel that one on your skin. Which line could you sniff?

show.text: The air stank of chlorine and hot chips.

steps.win: Yes! Chlorine and hot chips. Now you're at the pool. Writers call these sensory details.

steps.say: Careful! Zed's line says smelled. Is that enough to make it a smell detail?

options.reason: It is! Sniffing is a sense. Look at the last word.
Short is fine. 'It stank of burnt toast' is short too. What's missing?

options.text: It doesn't say what it smelled of.

steps.win: Yes! Nice is an opinion. Burnt toast is a smell you can almost sniff. Say what you sense.

steps.say: Let's fix my first try. Keep the canteen, but use senses other than sight.

show.text: The canteen was big and had lots of tables.

steps.ask: Which line puts you inside the canteen?

options.text: The canteen was very, very big and nice.
options.reason: Very big is still sight, and nice is an opinion. Can you smell or feel anything?

options.text: The canteen stank of burnt toast, and the benches were sticky with sauce.
The canteen had tables, chairs and a big blue door.
options.reason: That's a list of things to see. Is there a smell or a feel?

steps.win: Yes! A smell and a touch. Now you're in there with the sticky sauce.

steps.say: Zed says the best setting uses all five senses in one line. Read his beach.

show.text: I heard, smelt, tasted, touched and saw the noisy, smelly, salty, sticky, shiny beach.

steps.ask: What's the problem with Zed's line?

options.reason: Count them! It uses all five. Is it easy to picture?

options.text: Too many senses at once. You can't picture any of them.

options.reason: Beaches are great places to write about. Count how many senses are in one line.

steps.win: Yes! Two or three senses is plenty. Now pick your place. What would you hear, smell and feel?

terms.means: What you see. Good, but add another sense too.
What you hear, like whistles shrieking or kids slurping.
What you sniff. Say what it smells of, not just 'nice'.
What your skin feels: hot, sticky, scratchy or freezing.

examples.text: The canteen hummed with kids slurping noodles,
the benches were sticky with sauce.

card.test: Cover the sight words. Can you still hear, smell or feel the place? If not, add one.

weDo.frame: Indi is painting the footy change room, but she needs words first.
weDo.prompt: Which sentence puts you inside the change room?
weDo.hint: Which one could you smell and feel?
weDo.success: Sweaty socks give a smell, and the gritty floor gives touch. You're standing right there.

options.text: The change room reeked of sweaty socks, and the floor was cold and gritty under our feet.
The change room was a big room with benches and lockers.
options.reason: This only tells us what it looks like. We can't smell, hear or feel anything.

options.text: The change room was very, very nice and really good.
options.reason: Nice and good are opinions. They don't give the reader a single sense to use.

weDo.frame: Indi has a jar of details for her next setting.
weDo.prompt: Put each detail with the sense it uses.
weDo.hint: Ask: would I hear it, smell it or feel it on my skin?
weDo.success: Sound is what you hear, smell is what you sniff, and touch is what your skin feels.

items.text: Gulls screamed over the fish and chip shop.
items.reason: Screaming gulls are something you hear.

items.text: The whole beach smelled of rotten seaweed.
items.reason: Rotten seaweed is something you sniff.

items.text: The metal slide burned the backs of my legs.
items.reason: A hot slide is something your skin feels.

items.text: The old fridge buzzed all night.
Mum's kitchen smelled of garlic and wet dog.
items.reason: Garlic and wet dog are smells.

items.text: My blanket was scratchy and stiff.
items.reason: Scratchy and stiff are how something feels on your skin.

creature.name: Plumoth
creature.blurb: A moth with feathery feelers that can taste the air and hear a leaf land. It flutters close to any place that's described well.

workshop.mentor: The pool was already loud when we got there: whistles shrieking, little kids howling, someone's dad doing a bomb that sounded like a fridge falling off a truck. The air stank of chlorine and hot chips. I stepped onto the concrete and hopped straight off again, because it was hot enough to cook an egg on. The water, when I finally jumped in, was so cold it punched the breath out of me. I came up spluttering, tasting chlorine and someone else's sunscreen, and decided it was the best day of the year.
workshop.ask: Build a place from the senses. Ideas: Maxx's secret cage room, the footy change rooms, a haunted lighthouse, your gran's kitchen, Gus's slime lab.
checklist: I used two or three senses.
I added a sound or smell, not just looks.
I picked surprising details, not boring ones.
I made my reader feel like they're there.
